The system

Five roles, one loop

There is already a clipping economy, and it makes nobodies famous. Anonymous editors turn other people’s footage into followings, jobs and brand deals — with no rights, no credit and nothing paid back to the careers they are building on. We give that economy clean footage, permanent credit, and a payroll.

ArchivistsFind the footage, cut it, label it. Their record is public and permanent — it is the closest thing this world has to a resume.
EditorsBuild the mixes that travel. The good ones get discovered here the way they currently get discovered by accident — except with a track record attached and a name on every frame.
AIDoes the grunt work at a scale people can’t: proposes the labels, matches every clip to the box score, and builds the edit — cuts, ramps, transitions. It never decides what matters and never alters the footage.
Players & agentsPlayers own their archive and get visible again. Agents get a free, measurable publicity asset for clients who currently have nothing to sell — so they bring whole rosters.
FansGet the best history reader in sports. The obsessive ones become archivists, and a few of those turn it into a job — which is the whole reason the flywheel spins.

Confirm and file

The AI labels first and gets some of it wrong. The pay is for knowing the difference. Confirm what holds, kill what doesn’t, add what it missed; the clip gets matched to the box score in the background. This is the only version that reaches a million clips.

Raffles burn tokens; auctions take cash and split it with the player’s charity. Odds and entry counts stay on the card by rule. The best lots are access, not objects — a film session costs the player an hour, and the recording of it goes back into the archive as a story nobody else has.

The economy

One token, two doors

Tokens are compute credits. Buy them, or earn them working the archive. Nothing needed to contribute is ever behind them — they buy speed and scale. That, plus raffle entry, is what makes them worth money and worth grinding for.

InCash and labor

Token sales. Editors in a hurry buy compute. The margin line.

Daily

B2B contracts. Rights-holders pay to get their own libraries organized.

Contract

Auctions & sponsors. Cash for lots, brands funding prize pools.

Event

Corpus licensing. The labeled archive as a search API and dataset.

Year two
OutCompute and people

AI compute. Real cost per render — the token has a floor under it.

Per use

Archivist pay. Cash for verified work, separate from tokens.

Weekly

Prizes. Funded by players and sponsors, never out of wages.

Monthly

Charity. A fixed share of every auction clears to the player’s cause.

Every lot
Free forever SearchWatchClip & labelCut & transitions1080 exportEnter raffles you earned into

Buy the compute, or earn it.

Every token can be earned, so nobody has to pay to take part — that keeps the archive the fastest way in and keeps the draws clean. Paid entry into prize draws is regulated state by state and wants counsel before launch; the earn path is what makes it workable.

History of the Game09 / 12
10

Rules

Non-negotiable
Rule 01

AI never touches the footage

It proposes labels, matches box scores, times cuts and builds transitions — all of it on the timeline, none of it on the original. No upscaling, no generated frames, no invented detail. The record stays as it was recorded, which is the only reason it will be worth licensing.

Rule 02

Entries have no market

Prizes come from players — a jersey, a film session, a seat — and once you win one it is yours to keep or sell. The entry itself never trades, and neither do tokens. The moment either does, whoever grinds hardest stops winning and this becomes a speculative asset with an athlete on the front.

Rule 03

Credit is a resume

Every clip carries the name of who saved it, forever, on the site and on every mix it appears in. That record is public on purpose — teams, brands and agencies hire off it, which makes the archive a career ladder rather than a volunteer rota.

Rule 04

Players own their vaults

The archive is open to explore and build on, but each legend owns their own footage and stories — open-sourced in spirit, theirs on paper.

The league

What they cannot build themselves

The league’s history is its most under-used asset. This builds the thing they can’t: a living, organized, rights-clean archive with a fan workforce that loves maintaining it.

For the leagueDecades of footage finally organized, labeled, and searchable — by people, verified, at a quality money can’t buy.
For the playersRetired legends get bigger every month their archive grows — new fans meeting old greatness daily.
The dataThe labeled archive is also the best basketball training data in existence — an asset that appreciates on its own.
The momentStart with Baron and legends who say yes. When the mixes are everywhere and the archive is undeniable, that’s what Baron raises on — with the league in the room.

Sequence

One player, one desk, first hundred

One player. One desk. Real fans.

01Build the four screensBaron’s desk, working: folders, clipping, AI search, and the first mixes — a real site a fan can use.
02Invite the first hundredThe people already making basketball edits for free. Pay them for a month and watch what they build. Players come through their agents, a roster at a time, not one cold call at a time.
03Show, then raiseWalk in with a living archive, real mixes with real views, and legends asking to be next.
